utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then we can continue hereby immediately with the rebuttal phase of the closing arguments. The floor is for the Prosecution, please. But please, may I address both parties by saying that from our perspective, the purpose of closing arguments is not to fight against each other or to fight amongst the parties. I think the main purpose should be to convince the Bench, and I hope that we can continue this way. Thank you. Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, after listening to the closing argument of the Defence, I got home rather late last night, and I have a rather limited library at home. But thinking about some of the arguments, I did happen to find a passage that I found of some relevance to this case. This case is about Prijedor, and I think there's very limited value in any historical analogies, but given the arguments of the Defence, I think it's interesting to read that this is a cable sent from a western young consul to his ambassador on July the 24th, 1915. The consul wrote that "Everything was apparently planned months ago. First a few were said to have been involved in a revolutionary plot, and they were arrested. Some bombs were found, and further arrests were made. Those who were arrested were subject to terrible tortures. Orders were given that all arms of every kind must be surrendered to the authorities. At the same time all the leading men were arrested, the authorities insisted most earnestly that all who were arrested were involved in a plot against the government. Many hundred of the prominent men were thus cast into prison, and they were then sent away, and there seems to be no doubt that they were all murdered a few hours' distance from here. When practically all the men had been gotten out of the way and every weapon surrendered or found by the police, it was announced that all of the population must be deported." That was sent in Harput in 1915, but Your Honour, the point is that the Defence says the Prosecution has an imagination. We say that these crimes that happened in Prijedor were not, unfortunately, unique in history. What is unique in history, though, is that we have a Tribunal of international judges trying to look at the facts, trying to bring justice for crimes, horrible crimes, that were committed, in many case a very unique institution and obviously we all have an extremely serious duty and heavy duty to history, to international justice, in carrying that out. There are only a few points regarding the evidence that I heard in the Defence argument that I want to address. First, a few minor corrections: In the argument, there were -- there was a couple pages of references to Mr. Brown's testimony, and the Defence argued quite strenuously that the report in a Defence document, I believe it's D6, should have been reviewed by Mr. Brown, that his report could not be relied upon since it had not been reviewed. That report by Mr. Rahmic, who was a Muslim fighter. That report, Your Honours, is referred to in Mr. Brown's report on page 49, in footnote 242; on page 50, in footnote 246; on page 51, footnote 258; and in the transcript of his testimony on page 8602. So undoubtedly it was inadvertent that the Defence is incorrect when they argue that Mr. Brown did not review, did not consider, did not make that available to the Trial Chamber. I have been corrected. The document was D12. I'd like to also explain now something about Mr. Sebire's report, which was Document S281-3 that perhaps I didn't do a good enough job in my opening remarks explaining. That was the document - I don't know if it's still possible to put that on the screen - of the months of court declarations of deaths arranged by month. It's explained that figure 2 of Mr. Sebire's report on page 13 of his report. As I said in my opening argument, this is not the Prosecution case, that this graph and that these court declarations of death include all of those who were killed in Prijedor in 1992. Mr. Sebire explained in his report and in further detail in his testimony that court declarations of death are something that take place when family members come forward, it's voluntary, they come forward. They have to go through various procedures with the court. I believe there's a small fee. There's requirements. And then the court issues a declaration. So certainly the Defence is correct that the number killed in this chart, this only represents a survey, this is only a portion of the population that were killed. But it does show us a good survey of that population and when they were killed. Although the chart stops at October 1992, Mr. Sebire's report, I believe, makes it clear that there were no killings in November and December 1992 for which there is a court declaration of death. The report and this chart clearly shows the pattern of killings that began in May and escalated to its peak in July during the cleansing of the Brdo region, and then tailed off after the journalists' visits in August of 1992. A few other documents I'd just like to briefly address. In the SK46, the Defence referred to Dr. Stakic's statement at a public meeting in the municipal hall of the SDS in which he said, I believe, that the next two or three months are most important. The economy has to be revived. Peace must be maintained at all costs. Your Honour, it's never been the Prosecution's position, first of all, that Dr. Stakic or others in the joint criminal enterprise announced their intent publicly or outside of a very small circle. You recall even Mr. Zeljaja's interview in which he indicated that he had two different command groups at the barracks, an inner command and a larger group -- an inner command of only those he could trust. But further, Your Honour, if you look at the Prosecution indictment, what we indicate in paragraph 27 is that the joint criminal enterprise was an evolving one, not every person joined it at the same time, and the intent of that enterprise undoubtedly evolved. The Defence has not pointed to any statements of Dr. Stakic, once the real conflict began, the conflict that they were being -- that was being prepared, once it began on May 23rd of 1992. In fact, if you looked at S47, the interview of Dr. Stakic in Kozarski Vjesnik in 1994, I believe, he talks about what happened being part of a long, but for the Serbs, perilous plan. The Defence also presented a new document during their closing arguments. That would be D322. I'd just like to briefly comment. The reason that those SDS cards were presented was it was my impression from the Defence even as late as when Dr. Kovacevic -- excuse me, Mr. Kuruzovic was testifying, that the Defence was maintaining that Dr. Stakic was somehow not a member of the SDS. That does not appear to be the case according to the Defence argument. They don't seem to be contesting that. And I think certainly nothing that they have presented in D322 would change what I said in my opening remarks, opening argument. What it shows is that the accused was carrying until yesterday apparently four cards, calendar cards, with the SDS, three calendars from 2001, with the symbols and the representation of the SDS party. What the Prosecution has always maintained is that Dr. Stakic, once the elections in 1990 occurred, and he ran as an assembly member of the SDS, was a full member of the SDS, became its vice-president, and remained a member of the SDS all the way through the time of his arrest. In its argument against the genocide charge and the charges in this case about the plan and joint criminal enterprise, the Defence argues that there could not have been a plan to kill so many people because when Hambarine was attacked, why didn't they continue to go on and attack the other villages? I'm sorry, let me go back a little bit and talk about Hambarine, what the Defence said, for a second. First the Defence said that Aziz Aliskovic should have surrendered following this attack at Hambarine, what the Defence calls the attack on the soldiers. I'd also like to just remind Your Honours of the testimony of Dr. Mujadzic, that the soldiers, the wounded were lying out on the field, that he treated them to the extent he could without any medical kit available. Clearly, this was not an attempt to execute or kill Serb soldiers because the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. soldiers were not being fired upon; they were being treated by, in fact, the head of the SDA party in that field. The Defence says that Aziz Aliskovic should have surrendered. Even if we accept the Defence arguments about what happened and even if you accept the argument that Aziz Aliskovic should have surrendered, what the Defence doesn't explain is how that could possibly justify the attack on Hambarine. Even the Defence -- the Defence military expert, although he did not state it in his written report, admitted in his testimony that there was no military justification for attacking Hambarine, for destroying at a minimum 40 or 50 houses which the Defence witness saw just from the main road. Was there an armed conflict in Prijedor? Yes, we, the Prosecution, has always maintained there was an armed conflict in Prijedor. In fact, there were combatants, there were people such as Slavko Ecimovic who certainly was a combatant, who after the attack on the civilian population of Hambarine and after the attack on the civilian population of the Kozarac area led a very desperate attack of about a hundred lightly armed men in an attempt to re-take Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I take the liberty and when you are addressing this point, it seemed to be settled and it was not contested yesterday by the Defence. But still the problem remains as we hear it in other cases, do you regard this armed conflict as an internal conflict solely or also as an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have called this an unclassified armed conflict. We have not charged, Your Honours, the accused with crimes that require proof of an international armed conflict. The crimes that we have charged all require proof of an armed conflict, and the evidence has not classified it. The Defence has talked about the JNA being present, in fact they presented the Security Council resolution which called on the JNA to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina in the middle of May 1992. But for purposes of the charges in this case, it is unclassified because there was an armed conflict. And whether if there were external pressures on and involvement in the conflict or whether it was solely internal is not necessary for the proof -- is not an element of the charges which are alleged in the indictment. Clearly, there was an armed conflict. What I wanted to say about Slavko Ecimovic and the people who defended Kozarac, the allegation at least and it appears that Becir Medunjanin was helping to organise the Territorial Defence of Kozarac, that while they may have been combatants and under the laws of war they could have been detained, they certainly could not under the laws of war and international humanitarian law be tortured and killed, as they were. And perhaps this explains -- perhaps knowing what would have happened, maybe that explains why Aziz Aliskovic chose not to surrendered to the authorities who had seized power by force, not the -- legal authorities in Prijedor. The Defence then says that if the attack on Hambarine, if there had been an attempt to destroy the population, that the army would have gone on and the forces would have gone on and continued to attack. But Your Honours, that is exactly what the evidence shows. What we have shown in this case is that on the 23rd of May, Hambarine and surroundings of Hambarine, several other villages - you can look at the testimony of Dr. Mujadzic - was shelled for seven hours, and the very next day, Kozarac was attacked. Kozarac was attacked and thousands of people were either picked up and put into camps or taken away. The evidence shows that the attack moved on to the Brdo region in the middle of July, and it didn't stop until the visit of the journalists on the 5th of August. So the time period that we're talking about is about 75 days. The campaign that resulted in the deaths of thousands of people, the detentions of thousands of individuals in camps and deportations of many, many thousands all happened in a time period of about 75 days in one town, one municipality, Prijedor, thousands were killed. The Defence asked whether the attack was widespread and systematic. The evidence has shown not just the attack on Hambarine, which the Defence acknowledges; the attack on Kozarac and the destruction of Kozarac; the destruction of Stari Grad, the evidence has talked -- you have heard evidence about the detentions and the crimes in the Omarska camp, the detentions and crimes in the Keraterm camp and Trnopolje. But in addition, and perhaps it hasn't received the same amount of attention, but actually resulted in probably more deaths, the campaign in July in the Brdo region. We did have Ibela Atlija, for example, as one witness who talked about all the killings in his village, and that is what Colonel Arsic said was going to be the ciscenje in Brdo, a military operation, ciscenje. He even shared with us the photographs he took later of his village, some of which are now on the screen, S185-2, S185-6, S185-7, S185-8. Witness Q was from this region, talked about how many members of her family were killed in that operation. Witness S and Witness C. Witness G was a 92 bis witness from the Brdo region. And if I could just read one small paragraph from that statement on page 3, Witness G told us that: "It was clear that the Serb forces had started the cleansing of Muslims on Monday morning in the eastern part of Brdo area. They slowly made their way west hamlet by hamlet in the process executing Muslims by the dozens and pillaging every settlement that lay along the way. The Serb forces reached the western part of Biscani where lay Mrkela and Begici in the late afternoon." Nermin Karagic was from the Brdo region. I may have mispronounced his name and I apologise, in my opening argument. And he talked about how after the initial attack the people were waiting, that's the initial attack on the Hambarine region, somewhat hiding out, and then in July the forces came back. He talked about being arrested with his father, being taken to the stadium. We know about the massacre at the stadium. He carried his own father's body to the bus. He then was taken near the Kipe site, Redak, where another massacre of all those on the bus except for he and a few others who managed to escape took place. Even the Defence says this wasn't widespread in Prijedor and mentioned Ljubija, but one of the Defence's own witnesses talked about being in Ljubija and seeing over a hundred bodies on the side of the road. Men that had been executed. What the evidence shows, Your Honours, is that throughout this campaign, there was a coordination between the military, the police, and the civilian authorities. Evidence that the Defence does not address in their closing arguments, but which is clear, evidence that we presented in many different forms, orders, public statements, and documents. If you look at S107, it was a document mentioned by the Defence. And in this, this is the document in which Simo Drljaca orders the Omarska camp to be set up. He indicates on the very first paragraph on the orders of the Crisis Staff. The Defence argument is because Simo Drljaca indicates that the information should not be let out without his permission, that he's not informing the Crisis Staff about what happened. But if you look at the next page and the copies to whom this document is sent, the last page, the very first addressee is the Crisis Staff, and the evidence is clear in Dr. Stakic's interviews when he talks about Omarska, both in, for example, S187, in the interview with Monika Gras, he gives detailed information about the camps, about the numbers of people who went through the camps and were processed. In S47, the interview in Kozarski Vjesnik, Dr. Stakic talks about what was learned in interrogations. That's where he says "We learned in interrogations that there was a detailed plan where each neighbour had the Serb that they were supposed to kill. Each person knew which colleague, which neighbour they were supposed to kill." This was the kind of propaganda that Dr. Stakic was spreading. The Defence talked about the document from Simo Drljaca, D99. It's written -- I ask Your Honours to just pay attention, this is written in 1993 after we know that Simo Drljaca lost power following a revolt in the SDS in which Dr. Stakic and Drljaca, Ranko Travar were thrown out of office, forced to resign. In the article when Simo Drljaca complains Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about the civilian authorities, he clearly talks about those who were in power in 1993. In fact, he specifically mentions the president of the SDS, and we know from the evidence of the witnesses, particularly during the Defence case, that it was Simo Miskovic, Srdjo Srdic, those people who opposed Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca and who led the revolt that led to their replacement with Mr. Kurnoga and Radanovic as the vice-president of the municipality. If we could have S114 on the screen, please, and we could -- this is, Your Honour, an article, a document, very familiar again, not mentioned or explained in any way in the Defence arguments, about - if we could have it blown up a little bit. It's about the reporting on the implementation of Crisis Staff decisions. The first one that was blown up was the famous one about no release of prisoners. But if we go on, the Defence argued that there was no proof that the intervention squad was ever set up. No proof that Simo Drljaca ever reported to the Crisis Staff and Dr. Stakic. But if you look at the third conclusion on this page, it indicates regarding order number, gives the number, 17 June, 1992, the Prijedor SJB has established an integrated intervention platoon which together with the military police is actively involved in the prevention and deterrence of all sorts of crime. We heard about that intervention squad and what it actually did from Witness B who was present in the Keraterm camp, who talked about how they would come into the camp and commit crimes. How the intervention squad was present when the buses came the day the camp was closed and 120 men were called out and taken for execution. We heard about it from Nusret Sivac who said that whenever there was dirty work to be done in Prijedor, the intervention squad was always there to do its job, and they did it well. We even heard about it from the Defence's witness, Milos Jankovic, a police employee who talked about hearing the sounds of the tortures of the intervention squad, the loud screams in the SJB building, and specifically mentions Dado Mrdja as being one of those people. Certainly it is a key question in this case, key evidence in this case regarding the influence of Dr. Stakic on the police. There's all kinds -- there's a great amount of evidence showing the influence and directions Dr. Stakic gave to the police that were carried out. If we look at S64, it's a document of great relevance both to that question and to the questions which Your Honours will have to deal with regarding the accused's responsibility under 7(3) for failing to take action to prevent or punish crimes. If we can blow up this document, in this document -- I'm sorry, this is Article 6. If we can go back to the first article, perhaps I can find it. I don't believe it's blown up. This is a document which says that all Serbs imprisoned by mistake should be released. According to the Defence, Prijedor at the time was a victim of people committing random acts of horrendous violence. The Defence blames this mainly on refugees and drunken soldiers. And what is the response of Dr. Stakic to these acts of violence and all of the crimes and suffering that's occurring in Prijedor? He gives an order saying that all Serbs imprisoned by mistake should be released. And how is that to be implemented? If you then look at Article 6, and Ms. Karper can come back to it, Article 6 indicates that the decision would be implemented by Simo Drljaca, who would have the authority to decide himself on which Serbs would be released from imprisonment. So this indicates not only the accused's influence and interference with the police, but his interference and influence on the judicial system or his complete evasion of the judicial system, misuse of it. S84 required the SJB, the police, to submit information to enterprises on the inmates in Omarska and Keraterm. So over and over again, we see the documents showing the police and the influence of Dr. Stakic and the Crisis Staff on the police, on the camps, and on the crimes. According to the Defence argument, these crimes were committed by drunken soldiers, they were sporadic, random, uncontrollable acts of violence. If the Defence is correct on that, then you should acquit, if that's what you find. But does that make sense? Is there any doubt, is there any reasonable doubt or any doubt at all that all of these deaths in 75 days of thousands of people were committed as random, sporadic acts by drunken soldiers? Can we look, please, at S337. This was part of Ms. Tabeau's demographic report, and it deals with -- it has some information here about the populations and has information about deaths that had been recorded at the time she wrote this report and verified. She explained in her testimony what her sources of information were. The document shows that Prijedor in 1991 census had a population of 112.000. All of these municipalities from the Krajina region together totalled a little less than a million, 976.000 in population. The total number of deaths in the 19 municipalities was 3.010. Of those deaths, 1.747 occurred in Prijedor. We've heard evidence about how Prijedor was close to Banja Luka, Banja Luka was the centre of the region. Refugees went to that, the largest city in the Krajina, Banja Luka, and Mrs. Kovacevic talked about that, that Banja Luka received many, many of the refugees from Croatia that came. How did the number of deaths compare in Banja Luka to Prijedor? In Prijedor, there were 1.747. And in Banja Luka, there were 16. How do you explain that random, uncontrollable acts of violence are occurring on that scale in Prijedor, and on less than 1/100th of the scale in Banja Luka? The crimes were not random. You've heard evidence about the camps being set up, the organisation of those camps, the logistics. You've heard evidence of the attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac, the evidence of the Crisis Staff giving ultimatums, providing fuel and logistics to the army. You've heard evidence of transfers between the camps and the use of buses provided by the Crisis Staff. The massacres in Room 3 where so few of the victims have been found. It was not a random act of violence when not a single individual was arrested. The massacre committed by policemen from Prijedor on Mount Vlasic where 200 to 250 men were killed is not a random act of violence when not only is no one arrested on a convoy that was assigned to -- that group of policemen that were assigned to that convoy all day, but in which, unlike -- apparently the Defence made an error in its closing. The Defence said that the bodies had been exhumed. The bodies from Mount Vlasic have never been exhumed. 200 to 250 bodies disappeared. We have evidence of the mass graves all over Prijedor. These mass graves were not created by one or two drunken soldiers and people doing uncontrollable acts of violence. In Miska Glava, a site at the end of Prijedor, we know that the bodies were exhumed. We know that among those bodies were two women from the Omarska camp, Sadeta Medunjanin and I think it was Edna Dautovic who had been put on those buses in late July, 1992, and whose bodies were exhumed and identified by DNA. Testimony came from Mr. Sebire, from that Miska Glava mass grave site. Mr. Marjanovic testified, we talked about the site that was exhumed just about a year ago at Jakarina Kos where over 300, I believe, body parts were found. We saw that those bodies -- included in there, there were explosives, indications of some military hardware, and that the explosives had been dug into the rock using an expensive drill, a drill that I believe he said would cost -- I think he said 100.000, 200.000 dollars, that there were two of those that existed in Prijedor. The bodies were hidden. The evidence shows overwhelmingly an organised campaign, and I invite the Defence in its opportunity to give its final remarks to explain why in Banja Luka, 16 people are killed while in Prijedor, 1700 are killed. It's not -- the Prosecution does not believe that the people in Prijedor and the Serbs in Prijedor are different from the Serbs and people in Banja Luka. What was different was an intentional, organised campaign in Prijedor to exterminate and destroy the communities, to burn down the houses to, destroy the places of worship, and whenever possible to hide the bodies so that people simply disappeared. Intent, of course, it an element of almost all of our charges and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. certainly a key element, critical element in our genocide charges, knowledge and intent, and we'll explain in our brief the complexities of the various theories of liability. But let me make it clear that our evidence shows, we believe clearly, that there was this intent to commit these crimes and to destroy the community on the part of the accused, Dr. Stakic. In all of the crimes that happened, we saw the pictures -- we just from Ivo Atlija, we've seen pictures of Kozarac. We've heard about Stari Grad being levelled to the ground. We heard about the lines of women and we saw videotapes of the women lined up desperate to leave Prijedor. We've heard about how many thousands were killed and how many of them were known to the accused, how many doctors, his colleagues, who disappeared and were killed in the Omarska camp. How many prominent politicians and people he had worked with in the assembly were killed, tortured and disappeared from Omarska and other camps? We heard that the accused was well known in Kevljani, and we have heard the testimony of people like Sanja Poljak about the complete destruction of Kevljani, the murder of so many of the people of Kevljani. And we've even heard that the very person that Dr. Stakic replaced was taken from the camp and murdered, and that was Professor Cehajic. Dr. Stakic was elected in 1990 as the vice-president; he shared the office with Professor Cehajic until April of 1992. They sat next to each other at the Municipal Assembly. They both had full-time jobs, went to the same office every day. The accused was arrested in March of 2001. We've seen interviews in Kozarski Vjesnik, we've seen interviews with the accused on television, local television, interviews with the international press. When we look at someone's intent, the only direct evidence would be an admission, a complete admission of intent, which is rare. But one can view -- see someone's intent from their actions, and also from their words and what they don't say. In all of these interviews, from the time of these events in 1992 through his arrest in April -- in March 2001, we never heard the accused once talk about the crimes that were happening against the non-Serbs of Prijedor. The only thing we heard from him in all of these interviews were excuses. We heard justifications. We found lists that each Muslim had the name of a Serb that they were supposed to kill, telling the foreign journalists when he was asked about the Omarska camp and the killings in S187, remember all of the witnesses who testified for the Defence have talked about how people had heard about the killings, there were rumours all over town about the killings, we know how many of the accused's colleagues were in that camp and disappeared. And very nonchalantly in that interview, Dr. Stakic says, "Well, there were a few natural deaths." The journalist asks how many? "Well, I don't know. Not many." He was the president when entire sections of his municipality were being destroyed. When the population of non-Serbs went from 50.000 -- over 50.000 -- 49.000 Muslims, I believe, to 6, according to the Kozarski Vjesnik article in 1993, I believe that is -- if we could have it on the screen. I don't think it's necessary, Your Honours can view that evidence. Went from 49.000, and it's interesting that Kozarski Vjesnik reports upon this in 1993, to 6.000, to show that how much interest there was in removing and how many knowledge there was of the removal and destruction of the non -- Muslim and Croat populations. He doesn't once admit to the crimes in these interviews. He gives justifications. He tells outright -- he calls places like Omarska "reception centres." He tells outright falsifications such as in Trnopolje, it was a place where people could come and leave freely when we have orders from the Crisis Staff saying that no one can be released from Trnopolje without approval from the Crisis Staff. There were people who could leave freely, but there were also obviously people detained who had to get permissions signed by people like Mr. Kuruzovic. That's how we find person's intent. Your Honour, it's not easy to do, and it's not easy to look at a person and understand who they are and what they think. We learned that in this case recently, and we have seen people who come into court who look very respectable and talked about his great empathy for non-Serbs, for his brothers and sisters in Prijedor, and that was Mr. Kuruzovic, and we know he is nothing like the person he appears to be on first appearance. The reality is the crimes in this case were so massive that we can't imagine. That's true. We've heard from 40-so witnesses I believe or less, live in this court, from the Prosecution, victims, and the stories are very emotional and touching, but they are just a very small portion of the thousands of stories that were happening mainly in 75 days in Prijedor. The Defence called many witnesses who knew the accused, who had -- were friends with him. Mr. Prastalo still saw him in Belgrade, presented evidence from relatives, but none of those witnesses ever talked about Dr. Stakic expressing a single word, a single word of empathy or sympathy for any of the people that died. He didn't ask where Professor Cehajic was because he knew where Professor Cehajic was. He never expressed empathy for the destruction of Kozarac, for Stari Grad, for the thousands who were killed because they were killed according to a plan in which he actively and willingly participated. The Defence attorneys, I believe, have told us very sincerely that they -- the sympathy they feel towards our victims, but in all of his conversations with the press, with his own friends and family, Dr. Stakic never expressed a word of sympathy for the victims in this case. And Your Honour, I believe that evidence tells us what his intent was. It's interesting that in the Defence argument, they asked the Court to remember Mrs. Cehajic who testified and what she said about her willingness to trust this Court to find the truth, and that she wasn't prejudging anyone. But I'd like to go back to her words. And first, as I was looking for those words, I came across a question from Judge Vassylenko to Mrs. Cehajic at the end of her testimony. It's on page 3161. She was asked: "You were summoned for interrogation by the military. Soldiers were put on guard outside your apartment. Soldiers and policemen searched your apartment. Soldiers confiscated your car, and you were advised to request an official confirmation about the confiscation from the military barracks in Urije. Nevertheless, after the arrest and detention of your husband, you for several times tried to reach Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic, and not the police chief or military command. Why? Can you explain?" And Mrs. Cehajic answered: "The mayor was the person in the town who was supposed to care about each of the citizens." That was the first explanation. "And I thought they had worked together. And third, that he ought to know what had happened with his predecessor. And also, they took over the authority, and the person who had authority also was in charge of the police and the army, so it was all connected, who was giving orders and who was listening to, obeying the orders." Your Honour, Judge Schomburg thanked Mrs. Cehajic, as you do for all the witnesses for their contribution of your task of finding, coming closer to the truth. And she asked to respond, thanked you. And she said: "Thank you, Your Honours, Judges, who made it possible for me to do it. I would also like to ask you of course to take this into consideration in a real way and in an unbiased way, to judge to what extent who has contributed to what had happened. Who was not guilty should be freed. And who was guilty should suffer the consequences for what he had done." Your Honours, the Prosecution agrees a hundred per cent, as I know you do, with Mrs. Cehajic. If you believe the Defence case that these thousands of deaths were the result of random, uncontrollable violence, then clearly it's your duty to acquit. But the evidence shows otherwise. That is an unrational, unreasonable interpretation of the evidence that you've received of the coordinated, organised campaign involving the police, the military, and in the centre of the civilian authorities coordinating, headed by Dr. Stakic. Mrs. Cehajic said that those who are responsible must face the consequences of what they did. The suffering that was created in Prijedor in 1992 is unimaginable. I can't imagine really what it was. But it deserves justice even 11 years afterwards. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Let's hear now the closing arguments in rejoinder by the Defence. Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. What we do see from the evidence and what we can infer reasonably from the totality of the evidence is that Dr. Stakic is not guilty of the crimes alleged. The Defence has never taken a position that the crimes did not occur; the Defence, we had hoped, in a public trial by not subjecting the victims to further stress, pain, suffering, and possibly even humiliation, that that would be, and in my opinion is, a significant fact to show based upon Dr. Stakic's instruction and insistence to show what his feelings were with respect to those victims. That's the reasonable inference. That's, in fact, the undisputed fact in this case. The Office of the Prosecution would love to have had articles, interviews, and admissions. But let's be reasonable and see if they did, in fact, or if they were to obtain any such articles, would they truly, honestly, and objectively told this Court that sympathy and empathy is a Defence, and because Dr. Stakic felt sorrowful and saddened by the tragic events, therefore, you should acquit him? Or is it reasonable that a prosecution would utilise those statements and say it's an admission, that he knew what had occurred in that municipality and did nothing about it? The Prosecution is steadfast in maintaining their theory of the case. But when you read between the lines, when a prosecution -- a prosecutor tells you on a direct question whether something is an internal or international conflict and when they use the term "unclassified," it can mean only one thing. There is reasonable doubt. There is no such classification necessary. Either you take a position that it's an internal conflict or an international conflict of law. Multiplicity and duplicity, as we have argued in our motions prior to today, cannot and should not at the very least at the end of the trial continue to be utilised. Unclassified, without doubt, means there is reasonable doubt on that rather significant and important element necessary for the Prosecution to prevail. They discuss briefly widespread and systematic. What did Mr. Vulliamy say in his contemporaneous articles about widespread and systematic? Does he not affirmatively in August of 1992 conclude after a personal visit that he saw no evidence of systematic attacks? Should we accept that evidence? How much weight do we give that evidence? That is for Your Honours to decide. The theory has somewhat changed from last Friday, in my view. Now the joint criminal enterprise did not announce its plan publicly. It has been alleged that Dr. Stakic incited, inflamed the Serb population with speeches that would have been considered inappropriate, without doubt. They say that the joint criminal enterprise and this criminal plan is evolving or was evolving. Not everyone joined at the same time. The intent of the enterprise was undoubtedly evolving. What does that mean when a Prosecutor tells us that? That the facts do not exist in this case to convict Dr. Stakic. Is the Prosecution's theory that Dr. Stakic was the superior to the military? Friday of last week, they finally narrowed their position and said it was Mr. Simo Drljaca and the police. I think we can all agree unequivocally when we look at the evidence objectively, no one was superior and no one was subordinate from a civil, municipal, political level to Mr. Simo Drljaca. He took orders from no one; he did not respect anyone or the law other than himself. Was there evidence of coordination between the military, the police, and the civilian authorities? Mr. Brown, although his remit was rather limited, gives us those answers. He says "I can't tell you whether the police coordinated, cooperated with the civilian authorities because I honestly didn't review those documents." What he really meant, he wasn't given those documents to review. The Defence believes that the evidence is clear that only one reasonable inference can be drawn from the evidence, and that is that Dr. Stakic did not at any time possess the criminal intent for any of the counts in the fourth amended indictment. The Prosecution, as we contend, have tried to shift the burden of proof to the Defence so they challenge us from time to time and state "Why not in Banja Luka? Why in Prijedor"? Is there any evidence that military men were shot, ambushed, provoked, or attacked in or around the municipality of Banja Luka? None. Why? Because that happened and it was an omission by the Prosecution to bring forth that evidence? No. The only reasonable inference that we can draw from the facts is that there were no attacks on military convoys. There were no ambushes on military convoys. There were no provocations on the military in the Banja Luka municipality. However, it is not our burden of proof in this case at any time to prove a point or a fact. When we speak of cooperation, when we speak of coordination, the OTP continues to ignore the evidence, continues to ignore the evidence that the Defence brought forth as well as that the Court called. Was there one witness that the Court called that said there was close cooperation and coordination between the political, civilian, municipal authorities and any of those other organs? Do we forget the affidavits, the uncontested statements from Dr. Stakic's family supported by death certificates, mobilisation papers, when his nephew was killed? Should we draw a reasonable inference as once suggested by the Prosecution that it was proud -- you should be proud to be in the military, and he didn't want to necessarily ask for that individual to be removed from the military. And ultimately, his nephew was killed. Is that the reasonable inference? Or can we reasonably assume from the facts, from the affidavit, that genuinely, objectively, there is no doubt that Dr. Stakic had no influence on the military and could not even help his own family in any regard when it came to the military? Likewise, his brother-in-law, who suffered the same fate. Not one, but two critical pieces of evidence that clearly indicate that Dr. Stakic had no control or influence on the military. What about the live testimony of a witness that this Court will recall and that undoubtedly we'll cite in our brief who said she came to Dr. Stakic because her son had a Muslim friend, wanted him released from one of the detention centres. And Dr. Stakic couldn't help her either because it was not within his control; it was not within his power, and he certainly had no influence to release that individual or anyone else. The Prosecution does not answer any of the questions that we believe we raised yesterday. Was there effective control? Where are the facts to support effective control, if any? The only question answered is that there is reasonable doubt as to whether it's an internal or international conflict, by their own admission. The only question they answer is that the joint criminal enterprise seemingly does not and did not exist, because now their position is that it's ever-so-rapidly evolving from time and place, that they themselves can't figure it out. The reason they cannot figure out who were members of the joint criminal enterprise and when and where it evolved is because it didn't exist. When I use words such as "sporadic," "random," and "uncontrollable," those are not my words. Those are words that are in evidence. But it's hard to hear those words, difficult to find them in the evidence, most difficult to find them in the evidence from the Prosecution because Mr. Brown did not review that body of evidence. He did not review the military reports where the military and their daily reports, in my opinion, consistently and often cite to words such as "random killings," "sporadic killings," "drunken soldiers," "paramilitary drunken soldiers attacking civilians," "uncontrollable behaviour from groups within the military and those without". Those are not words that I chose to describe the events; those are facts. Undisputable facts that in my view the Prosecution continue to ignore as their experts have. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They discuss the May 15th, 1992, UN resolution to disarm. There is a resolution that discusses or that resolution in a separate paragraph discusses the JNA. Paragraph 5, however, is a separate demand from the Security Council, and as we placed it on the screen, it clearly states: "Demands further that all irregular forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina be disband and disarmed." What is an irregular force? Is it the Green Berets that Mr. Brown denies existed? Is it the Patriotic League that Mr. Brown denies existed? D12, the document that the Prosecution or someone in their office says it unbiased. When you weigh Mr. Brown's evidence and his testimony, see how much weight he actually gives to the document. Note that the document was not, at least the position at that time, was not fully translated, and the Defence did not have a complete copy of that 226-page report. An unbiased report by a Bosnian Muslim about the events in Prijedor, and its cited in a footnote, it's barely relied upon. In fact, it's summarily dismissed by all their experts. The illegal and irregular forces, did they abandon their theory, that is, as in most genocides the first step or the first thing you do is you disarm. I suggest to you that the Prosecution abandoned by virtue of their comments the counts of genocide and complicity in genocide against Dr. Stakic. I have no reservations to clearly say and unequivocally state that Dr. Stakic at no time was a participant in a criminal plan, a joint criminal enterprise which organised or assisted or cooperated with or otherwise coordinated this theory to "Destroy Bosnians, Muslims, and Croats in the Municipality of Prijedor." What other evidence do we have to say or suggest that Dr. Stakic had no influence, was not the evil man that the Prosecution wishes to portray? In a public forum in July, in a restaurant, when he met his schoolteacher, he didn't ignore him, a non-Serb. And Dr. Stakic, who is beating the war drums, deceiving Serbs in a public forum would embrace a non-Serb? What is the inference of that testimony? Should we ignore that testimony? We cannot, under the law. The only inference from that testimony is that Dr. Stakic did not have criminal intent as alleged for any of the crimes asserted in the fourth amended indictment. This Court, as I suggested, based on the decisional authority has the unique opportunity to render justice in a fair and even-handed manner. This Court, we would hope, and are confident in, will review all the evidence in its totality and will not allow unreasonable inferences to be drawn and unreasonable presumptions of circumstantial evidence to be drawn. This case is indeed complex. It's complex because on the one hand, not just the victims of the Office of the Prosecution, but the victims of all of us, of all society, these are all our victims, those victims on one hand are not to be judged to compare and necessarily say whether Dr. Stakic should pay for those incredibly horrible, tragic crimes. They cannot and they continue to insist that their theory, in essence, has been reduced to 7(3) and that Dr. Stakic failed to do something about the crimes. In order for the Court to reach that assessment, it must find Dr. Stakic to have been in a superior and subordinate relationship with one of the perpetrators or some of the perpetrators of that crime. He must have had substantial contribution and effective control over that which was occurring. We heard none of that testimony from any of the witnesses. All the witnesses uniformly and unilaterally stated that the civilian municipal authorities had no control or influence over the military. They had no control or influence over the police. If we talk about 7(3) and the police and we want to talk about the de jure alleged responsibility, what expert did they call to give us an objective review? What witness stated that they reviewed the police policy, regulations, and rules? In essence, they concede that point by virtue of not calling any such testimony and not having any such witness review those documents. De facto, whether they can prove that aspect of the case is also clear; they cannot. Instead, they go back to our emotional, our emotions and our hearts, and they dig deep and suggest that many, many victims suffered. That is not and has never been a dispute in this case. As the Court very well knows, from the outset, we did not and we continue to maintain that position, that we do not contest that those people suffered, that many were killed. What we do contest is the manner in which the Office of the Prosecution believes those killings occurred. In an organised fashion? One would think, if you discuss the Room 3 massacre and accept their position, that there was close to a thousand detainees in that detention facility, 100 to 150 were killed in the Room 3 massacre on July 24th, 1992. Was that organised? Was that foreseeable? What about the balance of those detainees? Can we take judicial notice of the fact that genocide was not found in the Keraterm cases that have been tried? Can we take or infer by way of judicial notice that the Omarska case that was tried, that there were no allegations of genocide or complicity in genocide against the camp commander or any of the shift leaders? Of course we can. Of course we know from those two adjudicated cases that indeed, these acts were random, sporadic, uncontrollable. We do not and we have never taken the position that Serbian refugees from Krajina committed these atrocities. We don't have the burden of proof, nor would we ever in my view suggest that a whole group of people, simply because they're refugees, or perhaps the Prosecution's position is simply because they're Serbs, committed these atrocities. What we hoped that we would have accomplished in this trial is break down the evidence for the Court, to view it in an honest manner, to review it in an objective manner, and then draw the reasonable inferences from that evidence. Dr. Stakic's comments that are so heavily relied upon by the Prosecution date two years post crimes that have occurred. We will find and we can find that certain issues of Kozarski Vjesnik do not exist; and undoubtedly, those publications were from the critical period in the indictment. Should we infer from that that Dr. Stakic said negative things, or should we follow the law where there's a presumption of innocence and that we cannot make such a biased inference because it is not the only reasonable inference from the lack of those documents being presented? If there are two reasonable inferences on a fact, the Court must, in our view, decide in favour of the Defence. If the Prosecution is sincere and they tell the Court "If you find that these crimes are random, sporadic, uncontrollable, committed by the paramilitary, committed by fanatics, by drunken soldiers, acquit." I direct the Court's attention to the military daily reports that were not included in Mr. Brown's remit. Accept their proposition and acquit Dr. Stakic because justice dictates that he, indeed, is entitled to an acquittal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution, is there a request for response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's not envisioned in the rules, and I would only respond if there's a particular point that I could assist the Trial Chamber on. I'd be happy to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. We will come with some -- of course not all -- questions immediately after the break. And it's at the same time an attempt to a certain extent to streamline the case and at the same time to try to get some more clarification on legal issues, but primarily on doubts the Trial Chamber has expressed in the questionnaire. And maybe based on this, the one or other point becomes more clear, or maybe even moot. Therefore, immediately after the break, it's our intention to start with the questionnaire. The two questions under III, seems to be limited only whether or not they uphold their allegations in these paragraphs mentioned there. But then, we'll concentrate on a question, and I believe that whatever the outcome of the case will be, initially it has to be discussed, what are the protected groups for the purpose of the definition of genocide in general and what about the targeted groups for the purposes of the definition of persecution and extermination in this case? We do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. believe that a discussion on these two issues will assist both parties in writing their final briefs. And then we will address only a few factual points, and these are primarily in the direction of the Prosecution. No doubt that also the Defence has the right to address these issues in response, but maybe it can assist us in shortening the final briefs. But as to the fact that we need to have a final clarification of the evidence before us before I can declare this case closed, I invite the parties as I did already this morning to use the remaining time, until half past 2.00, to clarify the issue on whether or not the Defence has had access to all the issues available within the Office of the Prosecutor of Kozarski Vjesnik. And please, let us know from both parties what the result of this investigation during the break is. The trial stays adjourned until half past 2.00. And we continue in Courtroom III. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.08 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. May I ask the parties, what about Kozarski Vjesnik from April through August 1992. Is there any solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I should correct myself first. We were not given access to the issues, if the Prosecution has it, from the 27th of March until 22nd of May, and two other issues, from the 5th of June and 31st of July. Otherwise, we received issues from June and July. So when I stated that we didn't, it wasn't correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. May I ask the Prosecution, what about the remaining issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're actually preparing a summary of what was provided to the Defence, trying to track down and historically recreate what was provided and what was missing. There was a list given to us, my understanding, from the Defence before. We located those that we did have, and we gave those to the Defence. We gave them access. There were two or three members of the Defence team who came and spent a few days going through those records. So I'm not sure if they kept records of which ones they saw or did not see. But given the information that Mr. Lukic just gave us, I know that declaration and that data is being prepared now. I shall email it from the court and see if we have a response about whether we have these particular issues or not. My understanding is all issues that we have have been made available to the Defence, but I'll double check that, triple check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. I think we have time enough this afternoon for this purpose. May I ask Madam Registrar, save the unfortunate missing documents D114 and D115, I think we'll track them down, is anything else missing, not admitted, translation missing, or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that we have the translation now of S430 and D305. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's hope that the two copies given to Prosecution and, no doubt, the Bench of D114 and D115 during Mr. Trifkovic's testimony can be found. May I ask the Defence, do you still have a copy of D114, D115?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar asked us yesterday to try to track those documents. But my search was unsuccessful. Fortunately, we have our case manager today with us, and hopefully we will have more knowledge and more luck with those documents but we need this evening to check that, Your Honours, because all our documents are in our apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We are looking forward to the same good news. Then, as indicated beforehand, we have some questions, and it goes without saying that related to factual issues, the burden of proof is with the Prosecutor, and therefore, primarily, the factual questions will be addressed to the Prosecutor. But no doubt, whenever the Defence wants to take the floor on a concrete issue, counsel may feel free to take -- to request the floor. As I said this morning, I want to start with the more easy exercises, and this is the question that the Chamber invited the OTP to consider, whether to withdraw the following allegations on the basis of that they are not sufficiently precise, and this would be the ones mentioned there in paragraph 54(3)(A)(xiii).

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just preliminarily remark that I'm happy to try to assist the Court as much as possible. As Your Honours know, there's about -- I think we are up to close to page, is it 13.000 or something like that of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: 15.000 and I'll do my best, based upon my memory and the collective memory of us sitting here, to answer Your Honours' questions. But more detailed explanations will appear in our brief, which we're still working hard on. As to the allegations in paragraph 54(3)(xiii), the Prosecution does believe that there has been evidence presented regarding Bosnian Muslim and Croat hamlets attached to the villages. I don't know if Your Honour wants me to go into the details now, but I can refer Your Honours to, for example, Dr. Cehajic's testimony, transcript page 3105, referring to destruction in Ljubija. Witness P, at page 3347, referring to destruction and looting on the road between Kozarac and Trnopolje. And also pages 3347 to 51, referring to houses that had been arsoned and destructed in Koncari and towards Trnopolje. Witness Q, on page 3930 and the following two pages, talked about destruction and looting in Ljubija. Witness S on page 5954 through 5975 referred to destruction and looting. Mr. Sejmenovic talked about burnt houses and destroyed houses on the road to Petkovci. I could go on, but as Your Honour can see, these details will appear in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Here, related to these two points, the question was only whether the indictment, in fact, this is no doubt a question where both the confirming Judge and the Prosecution's response before, that the question whether these allegations are pleaded sufficiently, with a sufficient precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that they were, and we also believe that in fairness to the Prosecution, that's an issue that should have been and was decided or should have been raised prior to the presentation of the evidence. The indictment is supposed to be a concise document, especially when dealing with hamlets in Bosnia where three houses may have the name of one hamlet, and you go down a dirt road another hundred metres, and there's a name of another hamlet. It would be ex-extremely difficult to precisely name each of those geographical settlements and some of them even contain multiple names. The Defence was put on proper notice because of the witness statements that were provided long before trial of the evidence. The indictment, we believe, was sufficiently precise in identifying these small hamlets in the manner that it did. And the other allegation was -- I'm sorry, which was the other allegation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 54(3)(B), during and after the attacks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we believe that is sufficiently descriptive, and it is what the evidence showed, that during, for example, the attack on Kozarac, houses were destroyed in the attack and the days following the attack, they continued to be arsoned, there continued to be destruction and looting of the houses. I don't know how we could have more precisely pled that unless we indicate actual days, but we do believe it was sufficiently precise for the Defence to fairly defend the charges and there were no complaints on the form of the indictment regarding that specific allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this clarification. Then, a more problematic point, no doubt, and it was discussed several times, but nevertheless, also in order that first the Defence has to prepare in the final brief and also in order what it's for us to cover, the question number 23 on the factual allegation is as precise as possible. Is it still the OTP's case that there was a joint criminal enterprise, or coperpetratorship? We're all aware that joint criminal enterprise is not yet a safe haven in the jurisprudence of this trial. It's just pending on appeal, this question, whether or not this Tribunal has jurisprudence at all on joint criminal enterprise. Therefore, we added the words "coperpetratorship" as one possible alternative, if so. But you may have heard from our previous comments that we have some doubts, especially whether it is the Prosecutor's case that there is such a coperpetratorship or joint criminal enterprise, both on a horizontal and vertical level. And if the latter would be true, what is the evidentiary basis for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, it is the Prosecution's case, and in fact, I think it would be unfair to the Defence for us to imply in this case that decisions were only made in Prijedor and there was no influence above. But let me explain that a little further. There has not been in this case, in the case that we have presented, we have not presented any evidence against Dr. Stakic, nor was he charged, with crimes that occurred outside of Prijedor Municipality. The -- in my view, and let me first give a little caveat because we are speaking of very complicated questions of law, as Your Honour indicated, first impressions. There may come a point in our closing brief that after reviewing my remarks, it's determined that the office policy was slightly different or I was unaware of a position or jurisprudence that existed. And definitely, our closing final brief takes precedence, and that is the office position, not my oral remarks, but trying to be helpful to the Trial Chamber. The key to the theory of a joint criminal enterprise and the responsibility of the accused is linking the accused to the crime. The links that have to be established, I submit, are in a downward direction from the accused through perhaps other members of the joint criminal enterprise, in this case, in Prijedor, the police and military, to the perpetrators of the crime. There has been some evidence, minimal evidence, but there has some evidence in this case regarding coperpetrators on a level of the republic and the region. But in our view, in my submission, the key is linking the accused, Dr. Stakic, to the crime on which Your Honour calls the vertical level, and I would say -- excuse me, horizontal level, and what I would call vertically down, linking him to the crime, it really -- we are not trying to charge him with any crimes outside of Prijedor under the joint criminal enterprise form 3, so we are not -- we don't need, in our submission, to link him to higher levels where these crimes were carried out beyond the borders of Prijedor. All that is necessary for our proof, we submit, is to link him to the perpetrators and, in the particular facts of this case, to his coperpetrators in Prijedor, the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But if you mention persons like Biljana Plavsic and others on a higher level, isn't it under the rules of logic the case that you, in fact, would hold Dr. Stakic responsible also for these crimes committed on a higher level, and therefore have this vertical link? Isn't it, in fact, the purpose of this joint criminal enterprise doctrine, with all the question marks behind it, that those persons - I remember Madam Korner elaborating on this - that the persons mentioned there in the fourth amended indictment may never even have met but nevertheless are mutually responsible because they are allegedly members of one and the same joint criminal enterprise. So therefore, if I understand you correctly, in fact, it's the Prosecution's case only that Dr. Stakic is held responsible for that what happened in Prijedor and has -- in the municipality of Prijedor, and therefore has nothing to do, and he as would be normal under the joint criminal enterprise doctrine, that he would also be responsible for that what happened in higher places. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Our case is limited, and let me just -- to what happened in Prijedor and by forces under the influence of the accused, and I add that caveat, because, for example, we do have charged killings in front of the Manjaca camp, the evidence showed members of the intervention squad on the 6th of August transferring prisoners from Omarska, killed them before they were allowed into the Manjaca camp, which is in Banja Luka. Similarly, the Mount Vlasic massacre occurred outside the borders, but was by Prijedor police, the intervention squad. And in that way, Dr. Stakic is linked directly to those crimes. As far as the crimes at a higher level, first, as a matter of practicality, we are not presenting evidence in a case where there's a joint criminal enterprise involving a great number of people of the responsibility proving, for example, the responsibility of Mr. Karadzic for the crimes. I think if we tried to do that, the Defence would probably properly object that the case is about Dr. Stakic and not Dr. Karadzic. What we -- we are not charging Dr. Stakic for crimes committed in Zvornik or Biljani or crimes committed in the Herzegovina region that Dr. Karadzic or others, or Srebrenica, that Dr. Karadzic and others in the joint criminal enterprise may have carried out. As a matter first of practicality and also in fairness to the accused, we are charging him only with the crimes in this case that he directly influenced in Prijedor as a member, we do admit, of a larger joint criminal enterprise. But we are charging him with those crimes directly linked through the horizontal joint criminal enterprise in Prijedor down to the actual perpetrators in Prijedor and from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would then be the factual and the legal link to the other persons mentioned in the indictment as participants in this one and the same joint criminal enterprise allegedly happened at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why is it necessary to mention and have the relationship to these persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, it was first deemed necessary because of a decision on the form of the indictment in the Brdjanin and Talic case in which it was stated that the Prosecution should name the other alleged members of the joint criminal enterprise. Is that necessary to have named those above the accused? Perhaps not. But then we only erred on the side of caution in giving the Defence further notice of the crimes than perhaps was necessary. It also, though, had some relevance in that part of the motivations and the policies -- we did present evidence that there was a motivations and policies for the crimes, to change the demographics to create a separate state came from a republic level, regional level. And I think if anything, it simply aided the accused in being put on notice of that, and probably helped the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber in putting on notice of why the Prosecution would present evidence, for example, of decisions by the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, of the RS Assembly, because we did want to put the accused on notice and have the Trial Chamber be aware that these crimes in Prijedor did occur in the context of a larger, wider joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It might be that the Defence wants to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. No doubt, we won't go through all the factual questions, but maybe it can be of assistance that we discuss item number 15 on the factual Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. allegations. That's a question of the evidence to support the allegation in paragraph 46 of the indictment. Asking for the basis for including the Prijedor JNA barracks, the Miska Glava community centre, and the SUP building in Prijedor on the same level as the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps. Is it still the -- still the Prosecution's case that these three buildings or areas can be seen as camps or in the sense as allegedly Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje were, or based on the evidence we have before us, to be extremely frank with you, it might be that at least the three first ones can be excluded right now because of the limited evidence and maybe that there's only evidence that the one or other person was interrogated there. But please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, paragraph 46 lists "camps and detention facilities." It has never been our intention to put all of these on the same level by no means. To be absolutely clear, and I think everyone in this courtroom knows this, the Omarska and the Keraterm camps were on a completely different level than the other facilities. Trnopolje was completely different than the other facilities, one, because of the size of the population; two, because of the type of acts and the frequency of acts that occurred, certainly the killings and beatings were on a lower level than -- lower numbers than in Omarska and Keraterm. But the number of persons held in the facility was much greater. The others were places where I think the evidence is going to show or has shown, people were detained for much, much shorter periods of time. We'll outline that evidence in our brief. But to directly answer your question, no, we do not maintain that these are all on the same level, and we don't -- we call them "camps and detention facilities." No way do we intend to imply that there was anything like Omarska and Keraterm in these other facilities that Your Honour mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So is it still your case that, as it is part of the indictment, that the Prijedor JNA barracks, Miska Glava community centre, and the SUP building were, in fact, illegal or not justified, even under the Geneva Convention not justified detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's not illegal certainly to have a detention facility. It is who you put into the facility. We heard about, for example, what comes to my mind at the moment is the Prijedor SUP building and people who were taken there, the people who were beaten there who were absolutely not combatants, in no way involved in hostilities, in no way could be seen as a threat to the authorities. I believe Professor Cehajic was there taken there -- Dr. Beglerbegovic I believe went there. Mr. Murselovic I believe went to the Prijedor SUP. It's not illegal to have a jail to put criminals, but when you detain civilians because of their ethnicity and beat them in that facility, then it does become a violation of international law in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same is true for the JNA barracks and the Miska Glava community, and you believe that you have the necessary evidence to support this allegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll address that in the brief. The barracks, I believe, were addressed mainly in the testimony of one of our 92 bis witnesses, and I believe there's quite detailed evidence. The Miska Glava, let me just see which ... I believe the Miska Glava community centre is the one that Mr. Nermin Karagic discussed in his testimony. But I think rather giving it off the top of my head and incomplete or inaccurate data, we do believe at this point that we have that evidence. We'll outline it in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Point 5, only for a better understanding of the Defence, no doubt we have written down this caveat, the absence of the question in relation to certain facts does not mean that those facts have already been established beyond a reasonable doubt. But there are some parts where we believe that maybe elimine they could be defeated. And therefore, we come back to point 5, and this is the question of the discriminatory element of the alleged denials of fundamental human rights. For example, the curfew, does the Prosecution really believe that there is enough evidence that the curfew was imposed on a discriminatory basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not our belief that a curfew is itself discriminatory. And although I don't have the exact language in the indictment in front of me, I believe what we alleged was a general denial of movement. The curfew itself would not be, we agree with Your Honours, that itself would not be a denial of rights if applied to all persons. And it does appear from the evidence that the curfew applied not to all persons, it applied to most persons and it was not only on the basis of ethnicity that there was a curfew. We do believe that the evidence shows a general denial of the freedom of movement, and that will be outlined in our closing brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But once again, is it your case that the curfew was imposed with a discriminatory intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's not our case that the curfew itself was the discriminatory intent, no. Our case refers to general restrictions of movement. Checkpoints where Muslims were not allowed to pass, what one witness described as the ghettoisation of the Muslim communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We heard several times the allegation of the -- of imposing a curfew, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just explain, add, I think we stressed many times the curfew not for the purpose of showing alone that the curfew was discriminatory intent, but to show the power of the Crisis Staff and the accused to impose orders upon the police which were then carried out. The curfew we believe was a very, very important piece of evidence, but it's not for the purpose of showing discriminatory intent. It's for the purpose of showing the accused's influence and ability to give an order to the police that the police then carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we come really closer to crucial questions. And they are ambiguous, both factual and legal questions. And this is about the protected groups for the purpose of the definition of genocide in this case. I recall that this morning, you mentioned related to the intent and also on Friday, related to the genocidal intent, the non-Serbs. Can the non-Serbs be a targeted group in the sense of genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe they certainly, can but let me be clearer. Our evidence has shown much more specifically that the groups targeted were Bosnian Croats and, in particular, Bosnian Muslims. In fact, the evidence is not equal. The evidence shows a greater targeting for obvious reasons of the demographics of Prijedor of the Bosnian Muslims. But I would agree with Your Honour, we have not produced evidence to show that all non-Serbs regardless of their ethnicity were targeted. We have produced evidence to show that the group targeted for destruction were the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear based on the authorities that only a concrete group, and if I understand the indictment correctly, this could be only limited to Muslims and to Croats, if any. So let us start with the Croats. The targeted group must be targeted for the genocidal intent in whole or in part. Is it the Prosecution's case still that the Croats, as a group, was targeted in whole or in part in the Municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know if you want me to elaborate, but the answer is absolutely yes. During the 75 days or so this campaign took place, we believe the evidence shows they were targeted for destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then this is now a real, not only academic, but a question that has been addressed in several publications on the question of genocide. Leaving aside the question of intent or knowledge and so on, but when you speak about Muslims, what is the targeted group? The Muslims in the entire world, the Muslims in Europe, the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims in the Municipality of Prijedor? And would this be sufficient under the terminus technicus targeting a group in whole or in part? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first we do use in our indictment the word "Bosnian Muslims" and let me first explain that the word is used in the sense of an ethnic group and not in the sense of a religion in this particular case because many of those people, we're using people who identify themselves or were identified with that ethnic group, not talking about their practice of their religion. As far as the group being targeted, where it exists, we believe there is jurisprudence in this Tribunal both here and in the ICTR that a genocide can take place on a localised case, the Krstic case and I believe the ICTR case, the Akayesu case. The evidence that we've presented in relation to Dr. Stakic, we believe clearly shows that the groups Bosnian Muslims, the Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in Prijedor were targeted by he and members of his enterprise for destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So for the purposes of the establishment of the crime of genocide, it's the Prosecution's case that it's related to ethnicity and not to a religion. May I ask, is the same true when it comes to the question of persecution? You may have seen that in several judgements, it was extremely difficult to make the necessary distinction on the targeted group. And what would be the basis for the discrimination necessary for establishing the alleged persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I understand the question, the group we are defining for persecutions in the same way that we define it for the genocide, the Bosniaks and the Croats. Your Honours understand enough about this area to know that people are very close descendents in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean coming from very similar -- I'm at a loss of words, very similar backgrounds, speaking the same language, identified themselves variously based upon the religion that they or their fathers or grandfathers or ancestors identified with, Catholicism, Orthodoxy or Islam. And that has an ethnic identification, whether the person was practicing that religion or not. There clearly was some overlap in the persecutions between seeing the people by their religion and their ethnicity. The question is not quite so simple, but that has been presented in the evidence, and I'm sure Your Honours understand it. There is an overlap in the region between a person's religion and ethnicity and how that historically has developed and been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So for the purposes of Article 5, you would make a distinction. It's also more or less a judicial hint because this Chamber is absolutely not clear on the scope of both genocide, the alleged genocide, and the alleged scope of what is called crimes against humanity, especially when it comes to persecution. The question is, is it the Prosecution's case, for example, when I see paragraph 54 where you can read the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Muslims, and then non-Serb areas.
