Would it be a discrimination from your point of view of all non-Serbs, be they now composed of Muslims, Croats, Ukrainians, and also related to their religion, but more or less making this discrimination related to all non-Serbs, or would you also here make a distinction and bring together the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Muslims, and others being non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there has been some evidence of people other than Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats being targeted. But that was, I would submit, because they were identified with one of those two groups, specifically I believe there was evidence of Albanians being targeted in one of the camps who were identified, our submission is, with being allies or part of the Muslim community even though ethnically they are different than Bosniaks. And one other case that comes to mind is the case of Dr. Sikora who was of Czech origin and we saw from the newspaper article where he was accused of sterilizing Serb women, I believe, that it was his religion that he was identified with and he was in that way seen as being allied with the Croats. It clearly is our case that the intention was to target Bosniaks, that is, Bosnian Muslims or Bosniaks and Croats when we use the word "non-Serb" in the indictment, and perhaps I think Your Honours could read that to mean Bosniaks and Croats, there were other individuals who suffered such as these Albanians and the -- Dr. Sikora, but it was because they were identified with that particular -- with one of those two ethnic groups that were seen as being the enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I regard it as only fair, because this Trial Chamber has not yet come to a clear opinion, leaving aside the mens rea for the moment, discussing only the actus reus, but it might be based on authorities that a distinction has to be made between genocide where you, in fact, need a concrete targeted group in whole or in part, whereas the crime of persecution following some authorities can be committed also against a group described in the negative. This would be a description of discriminating persons only for the reasons that they do not belong to the group of Serbs. And this group of non-Serbs be composed then of other targeted groups maybe in the sense of genocide, but I only want the parties to know that these possibilities apparently, following the authorities and in the last months, we have got a number of new authorities related to this, that there might be a distinction in relation to the groups in Article 5 and in genocide under the genocide convention. I believe we have addressed our doubts related to the question of the intent and the question of what is necessary for complicity in genocide both in our 98 bis decision and in the questionnaire. What remains for today is, maybe also in order to facilitate the final brief for the Defence, it's in 54, paragraph 5. Once again, we want to address that we should forget a word when it's on the denial of fundamental rights, we should forget the word "including," because what is not mentioned explicitly in the indictment, there the Defence has no possibility of defending against other allegations. Therefore, it would be first limited to the explicitly mentioned rights. But then the second question is, what is the fundamental right and what is the legal basis for believing that the right to employment or the question would be based on the evidence we have heard, the right not to be dismissed? Can this be really regarded as a fundamental right, as we have it enshrined in the convention on human rights on European level or in the covenant on a global level? Does this right is really such a fundamental right, the right to employment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the -- we have to explain this in a little bit more detail. First, I think there's a difference between being dismissed from a particular position, for example, if you simply dismiss the president of the municipality from that position, and denying a group all means of livelihood, all chances to find employment, discriminate against them in all fields so that they are no longer able to support themselves. And that is what we allege happened in the denial of employment. Further, in the particular circumstances of the former Yugoslavia, as in most former socialist companies or socialist countries in transition at that time, there were other fundamental rights tied to employment. Housing was normally tied to employment. Medical care, medical insurance was tied to employment. So it is our position that in the particular facts of this case where large numbers were dismissed from their positions, that in fact there was a denial of a fundamental right to employment that rises to the level of an international crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's easy to say international crime, but where is the basis for this international crime to be found in 1992? Where do we have the legal source that the right not to be dismissed is a fundamental right on the same level of as, for example, the right to life and limb?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would refer Your Honour to Article 6 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights. Article 26 of the -- I have just been handed this, and to be honest the ICCPR which means what I just said, the same covenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your understanding, the fundamental right in the same sense. Okay, I understood this. The right to proper medical care, do you believe that there is evidence that there was a discrimination related to the proper medical care, being aware that we have a lot of evidence that there were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shortcomings related to medical care and medication throughout the entire municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do. We can answer that much more better, in much more detail in our brief. There was evidence about what the care was like in Omarska camp, for example, that a person with a head wound, Dr. Sadikovic had to tie the person's hair together rather than just a simple needle and thread to stitch the wound together. We heard the testimony of Dr. Merdzanic about the children who were injured in Kozarac and them being denied the right to any medical care, and as a result they died, bled to death. The further evidence of reviewing the 15.000 pages of transcript we'll discuss in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But do you really believe that when a person came to death, that you have an additional allegation of denying of proper medical care?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that Article 6, paragraph 1 of the ICCPR, which I believe is the International Covenant for Civil and Political Rights which imposes upon all states the right to protect the right to life, that this would include the right to proper medical care, not being denied life-saving medical care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's right. But take it as a symbol case, when on a domestic level when you have a case of murder, would you at the same time allege the accused for having denied the proper medical care?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not in the same -- not in the same case, but there may be two separate acts. If one person fires a bullet, and the person has a leg wound, and the second accused prevents the ambulance from coming, prevents anyone from applying a bandage to the wound so the person bleeds to death, our position is that both would be criminally responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. Then we are coming closer to the point. Is there any discriminatory element based on the evidence adduced during the last year that you really can speak about a discrimination related to proper medical care?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe there is. One part of the evidence of that is the dismissals at the hospital. There is evidence that the hospitals continued to function throughout the time period, and our evidence, we believe, does show that there was a denial of medical care, sometimes of fundamental medical care to persons, particularly in the camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then finally, it's in the same direction, the question, in this same paragraph you mention the right to proper judicial process. No doubt, we have in Article 14 of the covenant and in Article 6 of the ICHR some fundamental judicial rights. But it's difficult to understand for us that on the one-hand side, the allegation is that people were illegally arrested, and at the same time there was no proper judicial process. Isn't this one and the same side of the -- of one coin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe Your Honour may be correct. It may be that what we're pointing out is that the Defence can't have it both ways, they can't say these people were lawfully arrested when in fact there was absolutely no judicial process. They were unlawfully arrested, there was no judicial process at all for most of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be a plea in the alternative. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, adding the caveat that I did at the beginning that our final brief may contradict my oral contributions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes it's only for an easier understanding. And then immediately emanating from this, I know that there's a lot of movement in the relationship between 7(1) and 7(3) of the statute. And also, in order to try to facilitate the work of the Defence and for our better understanding, how do you believe is it possible that you charge a person at the same time for committing a crime and then omitting to punish the coperpetrators and maybe the accused as such in person? Is this really possible to have both 7(1) and 7(3) responsibility in our concrete case? Wouldn't this be to a certain extent a vicious circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe actually that there's a lot -- as Your Honour knows, a lot of law in this Tribunal on the issue. And in fact what some of the cases -- and I believe it's Blaskic -- talks about is that some of the same acts that are failure to prevent crimes, for example, can rise to such a level that it becomes aiding and abetting a crime or it can rise to such a level that it becomes part of planning a crime or being a coperpetrator of a crime. Undoubtedly, there's a split in the trial Chambers and the jurisprudence about whether a person can be convicted under both modes of responsibility. But certainly, they cannot be -- and actually, there's even a -- I believe some of the Trial Chambers say of course you cannot punish for both, but I think there's a decision that says you can consider the fact that the person both aided and abetted or planned, coperpetrated in some way a crime and failed to punish or prevent in the sentencing, that dual convictions could be considered in deciding on the proper sentences. Undoubtedly, clearly there is overlap. This is a complicated case and it is a case involving the accused's superior relationship through a complex interrelationship between the military, the police, and the civilian authorities. We think that 7(1) does describe and the modes of liability do describe the accused's conduct; at the same time we think the accused failed to do anything when he had the power to punish the crimes, in particular to prevent crimes, that he did have the power to do that and nothing was done to prevent the crimes. Because we have multiple, multiple crimes in this case, we are not charging a single attack, when crimes are committed over and over again, it does become, we definitely acknowledge a blurred distinction between not preventing and planning and coperpetrating a crime itself, when you encourage that crime, when you continue to interact and support those committing the crimes and give excuses for the crimes, then we think you are both liable under 7(1) and 7(3). The question of whether the accused can be convicted for both and punished for both is a very complicated issue. If Your Honour doesn't mind, I'd rather not address that at the moment in oral arguments, but clearly there's a lot of conflicting case law in this Tribunal on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not surprised that you can't come to a final conclusion on this extremely difficult problem in the moment. And I'm -- I think I only want to address the parties that I believe there is just a case pending in the Appeals Chamber whether or not the responsibility expressed under 7(3) is a criminal responsibility that one can take as international criminal law applicable already in 1992. So this is an additional question to be addressed. And finally before I give the floor to my colleagues, I want to add one point that's not included, our invitation to address certain issues is also related to the following, the question of rape. We already discussed -- we already asked the question if there -- in case there would be a case of rape where Dr. Stakic would be responsible for, and this addresses also the question of foreseeability, but in a very concrete case, namely Trnopolje case, we would invite both parties to evaluate the evidence. We have here, which is extremely typical for these situations, evidence against evidence. (redacted). This would be the first prerequisite, that one could only discuss this issue. The second point --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think that was in closed session. I don't know if Your Honour wants to redact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't I mention the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You just mentioned the pseudonyms, but there may be -- can we go into private session for a second and I'll explain my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On page 8 of the fourth amended indictment, it is para 25, "came across such a notion and terms as deportation/forced transfers." Then on the page 12, we read in para 43, "the deportations or forcible transfers." And on page 19, para 58, we read "the forced transfers and deportations." How to understand all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, first of all, the indictment, and I think part of Your Honour's question relates to the fact that we charged deportations in count 7 and forcible transfer as a crime against humanity in count 8, as an inhumane act. The Geneva Conventions, as I recall, discuss both deportations and forcible transfer but make a distinction. Our particular statute has deportations, although they -- as a separate crime. And while it is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor that deportations as written in the statute should be read to include transfers inside a country, an internal transfer, or at the very minimum, it's our position - it's currently on appeal in the Kunarac case - that it should be over a border even if not recognised, such as the border of Republika Srpska, we believe that that's how deportation should be read. So far, the jurisprudence in this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber decisions that have come out have said deportation only, that definition only covers crimes across international borders. So if Your Honours, if this Trial Chamber makes the decision that you agree with our appeal in Kunarac that deportation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not in Kunarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In Krstic. In our appeal in Krstic that deportation does cover an internal transfer, we would be happy with that, with the following caveat, we don't know what the Appeals Chamber is going to do. So we would ask you to make factual findings. In fact, the facts of this case show people being deported across international borders to Croatia, and across an internal, nonrecognised border, that is from the areas controlled by the Republika Srpska army to the areas controlled by the government in Sarajevo. What we hope, in order to preserve our case on appeal, is that the Trial Chamber makes very clear it's findings of fact that both these types of forcible transfers across international borders and internal transfers did take place in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And one more question: What is meant by physical destruction of the group as envisaged by Article 4(2)(C) of the statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to be careful to give you a correct answer on this, so I'm going to look for the ... Basically, Your Honour, I haven't found the written answer, but physical destruction of the group means the death of the members of the group. It maybe manifested in a number of different ways, infliction of conditions of life designed to bring about their destruction. It does not mean the immediate death of every member of the group, but we do understand the term physical destruction under the law to mean the death of the members of the group. And that is the eventual goal. But under the genocide, it's of a group or part thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. A couple of questions, please. When you mention in paragraph 54(ii), you mention torture, physical violence, rapes, and sexual assaults, constant humiliation and degradation. Due to the very broad definition of the crime of rape in the Appeals Chamber judgement in Kunarac, if you take this definition, this broad definition of rape, what remains for sexual assault?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also refer you I think to the Omarska trial judgement, there's a couple paragraphs in that decision dealing with it. Kunarac, as I understand it, required sexual penetration. There certainly are many types of sexual assaults that would include crimes against a person where there was no actual penetration. And actually, that's addressed in the Omarska case. In fact occurred, and it's discussed in some detail in that decision. I will have to find the paragraphs for you. But our position would be that physical, sexual violence, for example, just to give an example in this case, witnesses talked about the day that the men from Brdo came to the Keraterm camp. I believe it was Witness B. He said that they were taken out, they were forced to disrobe, they were lined up next to each other, one behind the other, and forced to simulate having sex. Simulate that there was sodomy, but no actual sodomy. No proof of penetration or that actually occurred. That is sexual violence. Any touching that does not involve penetration, that's forcible, where a person is forcibly disrobed and touched in sensitive areas, areas of a private nature, we believe would constitute a sexual assault. So it would include a definition broader than Kunarac, because it is not limited to penetration, but would include other acts of sexual violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same line, you have the legal definition of torture in Kunarac. And so would that definition include the beatings as torture, or are those different things?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe those are different because torture has requirements that's not required in order to show beatings. Torture requires a purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Torture, then -- okay, thank you. But torture would require, for example, an intent -- well, I better read the definition of torture before I answer your question. I admit I am the weakest link. I don't know if I should walk out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's now for the Defence to address all those questions if they so want.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure if the Court wants me to address all the questions that you have in the guidelines or suggestions. But if we want to deal with the issue of genocide and complicity in genocide, I think it would be fair to determine what that group is. And when we say "that group," the Court did list out Muslims in the world, Muslims in Europe, Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also Muslims in Yugoslavia as a whole. We can't separate the theory of joint criminal enterprise without including it when we examine, in our view, the issues and the allegations of genocide and complicity in genocide. The allegations that are made in this joint criminal enterprise do go vertical and do go horizontal. It's not one way and it's not limited just to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prijedor. We submit that the evidence that they have tried to establish, that it's far broader than Prijedor, and that this Court in evaluating the group should evaluate it consistent with the allegations that are made in the fourth amended indictment, consistent with that which we were put on notice of, that there is a joint criminal enterprise, far broader than that of the Prijedor municipality. If that's true, and if they have alleged that Biljana Plavsic, Radovan Karadzic, Mladic, and others were involved in this joint criminal enterprise purportedly with Dr. Stakic, then the group is not limited to Prijedor Municipality. It has to by definition of their allegation be Bosnia and Herzegovina in its entirety. Similarly, if we read into their allegation on this theory of joint criminal enterprise "and others" or "among others," are they referring to Slobodan Milosevic? Of course they are. I think it's a rather straightforward assumption to make. If that's true, then the group has to be by their definition not just Bosnia-Herzegovina, but all of Yugoslavia or former Yugoslavia. In order to examine fairly what group or part of group they contend that Dr. Stakic is culpable for, discriminated against, and quite frankly intended to destroy, it's all the Muslims, all the Croats, all the non-Serbs in the entirety of the former Yugoslavia. That's their allegation. It's in their indictment. They have not withdrawn it, despite invitations to do so. That's the group that this Court must consider first and foremost in reaching any decisions on actus reas. We submit that in their contentions for limiting the group and saying intellectuals or educated people and citizens were targeted, they have not proved that, it's an alternative plea. But once again, the scope of that group should not be limited to the Prijedor Municipality or just Bosnia and Herzegovina, and perhaps not just the former Yugoslavia as well. It is extremely complicated, although we have been put on notice that it's all Muslims, Bosniak Muslims can live in other countries, do live in other countries. In Germany, when you identify or when you ask someone what is he, they say: "I'm a Bosnian Muslim," but they live in Germany. In America, I have personally experienced that. They've obtained American citizenship, and they still identify themselves as Bosnian Muslims, proudly and rightly so. However that's the group that this Court must examine in determining what the actus reas was in this case based on their allegations and whether or not genocide was perpetrated and whether or not there was complicity in that purported genocide, to destroy with intent all Bosnian Croats and all Bosnian Muslims, and the non-Serbs. I also believe, Your Honour, although there is decisional authority that I'm sure we're all anxiously awaiting from other appellate decisions, we must contrast the difference between genocide and complicity. You can't have a definition of complicity to include aiding and abetting, because the statute itself has a specific paragraph and specifically mentions aiding and abetting as a crime. To have an affirmative act, direct participation, or a secondary participation, we must contrast that, direct perpetrators with secondary perpetrators, both when you aid and abet or directly intend and commit those crimes, it's relatively straightforward that there must be affirmative action. What we have here is allegations of omissions, allegations of complicity in a plan that we suggest has not been proven to kill all Muslims and Croats in the territory of former Yugoslavia, or even Bosnia and Herzegovina, or even in Prijedor Municipality. Specifically, when we discuss complicity, the individual must not only be a participant or have knowledge of these what I consider to be rather broad and loose facts which somehow can be reached or concluded to be genocide, the individual, Your Honour, has to know and acquiesce to that plan. The individual has to specifically understand the plan. The individual in my view has to directly acknowledge the plan and directly and openly submit to the furtherance of that plan. What we're doing with respect to knowledge and complicity, I would say, in the arguments that I have heard is reducing that very, very serious crime, as in most of the literature and as the Court cites in its decision on 98 bis, the crime of all crimes, genocide as well as complicity in genocide, we're reducing the level necessary to prove someone's guilt on that by way of academic issues. We're saying that all a person needs to get convicted of genocide or complicity of genocide is knowledge of a bad act, of a terrible act, of a horrific act. If that's true, are we all not regrettably in some way complicit in that which occurs throughout the world if we don't affirmatively react immediately to it. How remote will the definition become if knowledge is the sole requirement for complicity in genocide? I submit the case law does not state that knowledge without specific mens rea is necessary. I think criminal mens rea is necessary for complicity in genocide as well. On actus rea, this Court, in determining which group in whole or in part or as such is the group that should be examined should refer in my view to the Keraterm and Sikirica opinion, and not the ICTR opinion in Musema [sic]. I think that opinion clearly defines how it is that you can reach a group or determine what that group is, despite alternative theories and pleadings by the Prosecution. That case clearly held that you cannot continue to limit a group and ultimately only argue the targeted group that the genocide perpetrators wanted to exterminate were those that they exterminated. Extending that logically to its most ridiculous level, we would say that genocide can occur in the killing of five, three, one individual. Does it still become genocide? Is there a difference between massacres and genocide? Is there a difference between murder and genocide? We believe, Your Honour, in this case those are critical and very vital issues of utmost importance. We believe the group is far broader than that just limited in the Prijedor Municipality. We do not believe that it's all Muslims in the world. I cannot tell the Court with all honesty if it doesn't mean all Bosnian Muslims throughout the world. It makes some sense if the allegation is that there is an intent to destroy Bosnian Muslims, that that does indeed mean all Bosnian Muslims throughout the world. However, if we look at the Sikirica opinion and the rationale in Sikirica, we can find, we believe, that the group and the analysis there will be of great benefit and assistance in determining the issues of genocide and complicity in genocide. It is, I believe, the only case where complicity in genocide was discussed and was alleged in the former Prijedor Municipality in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I be so impolite, for technical reasons we need a break now the tape has to be exchanged. How many minutes do we need? Three minutes? Would it be sufficient? So please, we are waiting in front of the courtroom. The trial stays adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And sorry for the interruption, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we will obviously attempt to cover this complicated and very difficult issue of complicity in genocide in our brief, but it is important even when you examine the court's 98 bis decision in paragraph 26 of that decision where the court says that acts can be elevated to genocide if the perpetrator wants the desired result. We submit when the question of intent, criminal intent, the mens rea for genocide must be proven, not just by virtue of knowledge of actions. When the Court uses the word "want" in paragraph 26 of its decision, want in my view is a desire, a wish, an intent. You must intend, and you must prove that the accused had the necessary criminal mens rea to be convicted of complicity in genocide or genocide. I know this Court has given us significant judicial hints with respect to many issues, as well as our conduct. However, I must add that this Court did take the position that we should examine first the actus Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reas to determine whether it existed, and then fall back on evaluating the evidence when it comes to the mens reas. We believe that the Sikirica decision determines properly, in our view, states that first determine if there's a mens rea and then proceed with the evaluation of the protected group, et cetera. But we'll address that, I hope, in a little more detail in our brief. The question was asked, what is a fundamental right? We can argue that all individual rights are fundamental in one way or another. However, when the international criminal jurisprudence suggests and uses the word "fundamental right," I do not believe since the Office of the Prosecution has admitted the case is confined to 75 days or 72 days, whatever the number was, less than 90 days, is it a fundamental right of employment not to be dismissed for employment? All those rights may be -- or judicial process may be at some point over a longer period of time constitute fundamental rights, but the question is do the violation alleged of those rights for that 75-day period constitute a fundamental right? Does not the Geneva Convention suggest that you may detain a suspect during a conflict for 90 days? Is it a breach of that fundamental right of judicial process if you release that detainee within that 90-day period? We hope to address that with some more clarity in our brief. The Honourable Judge Vassylenko raised the question of deportation and forced transfer. When we evaluate that, we hope to evaluate what role the international community as a whole played in removing individuals from the municipality, whether it be from Trnopolje Detention Centre or camp to other parts of former Yugoslavia or other parts of the world. I don't know that I'm prepared to quantify the numbers. There has been some testimony that after the 6th of August, 1992, the Red Cross -- the International Red Cross was permitted to go to the detention centres and the camps and, without overstating the evidence, in some way either assisted, guided the transfer of some of these individuals from the Prijedor Municipality to other parts of the world. In order to determine those issues of deportation and/or forcible transfer, we must examine that evidence. Or do we really quantify it in another manner? We hope to address that specific issue in our brief. I'm thankful that the intent to destroy and/or physical destruction of a group, it is another stipulated fact. We agree that if a criminal plan with the intent to destroy or the words "physical destruction" undoubtedly means death. That, I think, is a fact, and that is the way I think both parties are proceeding. We do have obviously many comments with respect to the Court's memo issues that need to be addressed. We expect fully to address them in our brief, and if necessary, in our reply once we obtain the Prosecution's final brief. If necessary or if the Court has any specific questions, we would be happy to address the Court on those today or at any time thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is there anything to be added by one of the parties before we come to the last word of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll just say briefly that the law is absolutely clear in the ICTR jurisprudence, complicity in genocide does not require on the part of the accused on trial a specific intent to destroy the group. The mens rea of the accused would only be knowledge of the crime and knowledge of the specific intent of others perpetrating the crime. When the statute of this Tribunal was set up, it's our position that it was not the intent of the authors to limit the definitions of genocide and the modes of responsibility so as to cover as little and as few people as possible; rather, the intent was to protect societies from genocide. For that reason, Article 4 of the statute includes modes of liability and inchoate offences not included in 7(1) such as conspiracy to commit genocide and attempt to commit genocide and complicity to commit genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But only that the parties are aware, the question we have before us is whether or not in 1992, one could really speak about international criminal law applicable at that time to a certain extent going beyond that what has been at that time the jurisprudence under the genocide convention of 1948. We should be aware of this problem and the problem that maybe something has been added, especially with the words "aiding and abetting." But we all know that we have a number of authorities, and unfortunately a number of different decisions on this issue, and it will be extremely difficult for the Appeals Chamber to bring all these decisions at one day under one roof without sending them back. I think we have heard evidence. I would have appreciated if we could have had the chance to discuss also orally legal questions a little bit more. But sometime the day has come and the time has come that we are close to the end of the case, and as it is the custom in most continental European countries, and also in former Yugoslavia and here in the Netherlands, I think it is important to get a final impression of that what the accused. And I started this case by stating the main person in this case is Dr. Stakic, what Dr. Stakic has to tell us at the end of this case. May I therefore ask that Dr. Stakic please take the seat where normally the witness takes a seat, that he can address us directly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all those present in this courtroom. The indictment against me was written in horrendous manner, and it struck deep. It hit me hard. It struck me even harder than the very fact that I am detained in a prison. Regardless of the outcome of this trial, this is something which will stay with me until the end of my life. Unfortunately, my family will also be affected. This very fact as well as another one; namely, the distortion and misinterpretation of my words, the words I said, in newspaper interviews, all this has fortified me in my decision to invoke my right to remain silent so as not to be subjected to further distortions of my words by the Office of the Prosecutor. However, the way the Trial Chamber has treated me from day one to this very day, regardless of anything that is alleged in the indictment, the Trial Chamber has always seen in me primarily a human being. That is my honest impression. I am in a way for this very reason indebted to address you with a few words. Firstly, in order to tell you about my deepest regret for everything that happened in the area of Prijedor Municipality, and this goes to all citizens of Prijedor Municipality, I would also like to say that I grew up in peace. I became a grown person in peace. I was raised in my family not to argue with my neighbours. When I started going to primary school, we had a mixed group of both teachers and children there. All children were the same I was taught regardless of which God they prayed to. I was taught that this should not be held against them because that could not be held against them in any way that would have been permissible. As a boy, I used to travel to Slovenia to the Slovene coastline where my aunt lived. When I was 12, I went to Trieste in Italy. When I was 15, I first went to Germany. I served my military service in the JNA in Skopje Macedonia. I know what freedom means. As for war, I read about war in domestic literature and in foreign, international literature too. I watched movies. I pictured war as something horrendous. Regardless of the fact that back then, there were wars in the world, in Asia, in Africa, I believed, I was deeply convinced that no such thing would ever be possible in Europe. I never believed it could happen in my country, in Yugoslavia, which is part of Europe. Unfortunately, it did happen. All I can tell you is that the reality of that war was more horrible than anything I could read in books. Who can be in control in a situation like that? The first fallen person, the first person who was killed in Prijedor Municipality, was a young man, aged 18. A Muslim young man. He was killed in Slovenia in early summer of 1991. This was not a death in a pawnshop or in a car accident. He was a member of the JNA which still existed. And he was killed by members of Jansa army or the Slovene army, whatever its name was. Someone had to go to the family and express their condolences. On one hand, the duties of the president of the assembly in peacetime, he presides over the sessions of the assembly, he attends the ceremonies in companies, in cultural associations, in sports clubs or if a factory is being opened, if a new road is being opened. In wartime, what it mostly boils down to is expressing condolences to the families of those killed, the care of invalids and handicapped people, the care of families so that an invalid person can access their own home, and all the other vicissitudes. The war did happen. A number of crimes did happen in that war. As my attorney said, it wasn't their aim or my aim here to prove that no crimes ever occurred. Our aim, rather, was to try to show this Tribunal and the public at large that I was no part to those crimes, and especially not -- especially to show that I did not instigate, aid, and abet any of those crimes. I can only ask myself whose conclusion was that and on the basis of what was that conclusion reached? I did hear of some of the crimes even during the war. Some of the crimes I only learned about to tell you the truth here in this courtroom. But I had no real power ever to effect or influence any of those crimes, to prevent them or to punish the perpetrators. I was not even in a position to issue an order to the communal inspector, the municipal inspector, to go to an open-air market or a bar to carry out an inspection. I simply didn't have the authority to do that. It was outside my own purview, outside my own jurisdiction. All the same, I would like to thank each and every one of the witnesses who came here to testify and help each in their own way to in some way get as close as possible to the truth of what really happened there. Although I would like to note just briefly that I was not present at all the places that the witnesses claimed I was. Once again, I would like to say that everyone was the loser in this war, no matter if they were hurt or killed personally or if they lost members of their family, they lost a limb or were maltreated in any way or if their house was destroyed. What I want to do and what I can do is to express my deepest regret to all citizens of Prijedor. When I say "all," this comprises Croats, Serbs, Muslims, and all the other ethnic minorities living there, or rather, who lived there. Once again, may I be allowed to express my debt of gratitude to this Trial Chamber for the fair way in which they treated me. I also want to thank all the other participants in this trial whom I may have observed at certain points a bit too obtrusively. I tried to look into their eyes. I wanted to see, I wanted to find out how they were looking at me and when they were looking at me, what they were seeing. I have nothing further to add except express my thanks yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, take your seat again. Now, after exactly 150 days and exactly one year of hearings, we started the 16th of April, today the 15th of April, having heard witnesses from all areas, all backgrounds, on more than 15.000 pages of transcripts, having before us about 1.500 exhibits, having taken a number of depositions, videolinks, 92 bis witnesses, it is now to find the facts, to find the applicable law, and then to find out what about the accusations in the fourth amended indictment. I hope that the participants will present their views as precise as possible in the final briefs to be expected as scheduled for the 28th of April. And it is on purpose that we granted additional days, until the end of that week, that in case the one or other party, but in this case, especially the Defence, believes to be taken by surprise, that there is a possibility to respond to this. As I mentioned this morning, we can't promise when we can hand down the judgement. It's by experience, and I know how difficult it is for an accused and the family of an accused, to wait for the judgement in the first instance. So we'll try to do our very best, but we don't want to make any promise. But ask the parties to be prepared by the end of July this year in case we are ready until then to hear the judgement. Following Rule 87 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I declare hereby the hearing closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 4.41 p.m.
